c.tagline: St-Barth's yacht-filled harbour capital of Swedish-era forts, designer boutiques and the golden sand of Shell Beach.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps on St-Barth. A small fleet of licensed taxis uses government-set zone fares, with surcharges at night and on Sundays and holidays. Book by phone or use the ranks at the airport and in Gustavia; most visitors rent a car or an open-sided mini-moke.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number reaching police, fire and ambulance. The island hospital, Hôpital de Bruyn, is in Gustavia.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Flamands: Anse des Flamands beach, Saint Barthélemy

hood_desc: The red-roofed Swedish-era harbour capital, where megayachts moor along a waterfront ringed by luxury boutiques (Hermès, Louis Vuitton, Cartier), gourmet restaurants and the hilltop ruins of Fort Karl and Fort Gustav; the walkable hub for shopping, dining and the town's own Shell Beach a short stroll away.

The island's lively main beach and commercial heart, famously split by the short, steep-approach airport runway; boutiques, beach clubs (Nikki Beach, Eden Rock) and casual bistros draw a stylish, see-and-be-seen crowd.
A broad, dramatic white-sand beach on the northwest coast backed by discreet luxury hotels and hillside villas; scenic, less crowded and a relaxed base for an upscale barefoot stay.

A shallow, reef-protected turquoise lagoon on the east coast, ideal for families, kitesurfing, windsurfing and paddleboarding, with beachfront hotels and restaurants tucked between the water and Morne du Vitet.
A laid-back local village with a calm family beach, a well-known surf break, small grocers and a more authentic, residential feel than the resort areas.
lodging: Cheval Blanc St-Barth Isle de France

water.note: Desalinated tap water is safe to drink, though many prefer bottled.

transit.pay: There is no public bus or rail on St-Barthélemy. Licensed taxis charge fixed zone fares (with night and Sunday surcharges), paid in cash or card. Most visitors rent a car, scooter or mini-moke.
transit.hours: Taxis run on demand; arrange pickups by phone in advance, especially at night when the small fleet is limited.
transit.note: St-Barthélemy has no public transport network. Getting around is by rental car, scooter or open-sided mini-moke, or the island's small licensed-taxi fleet; taxi ranks sit at the airport and in Gustavia.

car.idp: Not required for EU or US licenses; a valid national driving licence is accepted

tip.r: A service charge is generally included ('service compris'); rounding up or leaving 5-10% extra for good service is appreciated but not required.

landmarks: Gustavia Harbor
Mega-yachts and red-roofed Swedish colonial buildings ring this perfect horseshoe port, the glamorous heart of St. Barth where café terraces meet designer boutiques.
Shell Beach (Plage de Shell Beach)
A five-minute stroll from downtown, this cove carpeted in millions of tiny seashells offers swimming, sunset cocktails and cliff-jumping right on Gustavia's doorstep.
Fort Karl
The short hike to these hilltop Swedish fort ruins rewards with the island's best panorama over Shell Beach, Gustavia harbor and anchored superyachts.
Gustavia Lighthouse and Fort Gustav
Above the harbor's northern edge, a squat red-and-white lighthouse stands amid 18th-century Swedish fort remnants, commanding sweeping views across town and the Caribbean.
Wall House Museum (Territorial Museum)
Housed in a restored 18th-century stone warehouse on the harbor, this museum traces St. Barth's Swedish, French and seafaring past through maps, costumes and artifacts.
St. Bartholomew's Anglican Church
Built in 1855 of local stone and limestone shipped from St. Eustatius, this charming seafront church is Gustavia's most photographed historic facade.
Notre-Dame de l'Assomption Catholic Church
This 1829 Catholic church with its freestanding bell tower and coral-stone walls anchors Gustavia's old quarter in quiet Swedish-era elegance.
Fort Oscar
Guarding the harbor mouth from the Petits Saints promontory, this 17th-century fortification—now housing the gendarmerie—makes a striking landmark on Gustavia's skyline walkabout.
Rue de la République and Quai de la République
Gustavia's chicest streets line the waterfront with Hermès, Cartier and pastel Creole cottages, a duty-free shopping promenade unmatched in the Caribbean.
Anse de Colombier (Colombier Beach)
A short drive and scenic cliff trail from town leads to this boat-or-hike-only white crescent, the island's most pristine bay for snorkeling among turtles.

train.note: There is no railway on St Barth. Arrive by air into Gustaf III Airport - a famously short runway served only by small aircraft from St Maarten and Guadeloupe - or by ferry from Sint Maarten.

bus.note: There is no public bus service at all on St Barth. Visitors hire cars, mini-mokes or scooters, or use taxis, which operate on fixed rates. The island is small enough to drive end to end in half an hour.

intl.to: Philipsburg & Marigot, Sint Maarten / Saint-Martin - ~45 min

ferry.note: The fast ferries to St Maarten are the main sea link and the cheaper alternative to the small-plane hop, taking about 45 minutes from Gustavia's harbour with several departures a day. It is an international crossing between French and Dutch territory, so carry your passport. The channel is exposed and crossings can be rough in winter - motion sickness is common.

half.name: Île Fourchue
half.blurb: Uninhabited volcanic islet off the coast, with a protected cove for snorkeling among coral and passing eagle rays.

half.name: Saint-Martin
half.blurb: Twin-nation island reachable by ferry, split between French and Dutch sides with different beaches and shopping streets.

full.name: Anguilla
full.blurb: British territory known for white-sand beaches, reached from St. Barts by a boat crossing open water.

full.name: Saba
full.blurb: Volcanic Dutch Caribbean island with no beaches, known instead for steep hiking trails and wall diving.
